newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin takes gamble by promoting Chubais.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin takes gamble by promoting Chubais.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's decision to appoint Anatoly Chubais to a key government post indicates the combative Russian leader considers the need to further reforms more important than opposition outrage.

Political battles are Yeltsin's preferred modus vivendi and, now he appears recovered after eight months of heart illness followed by pneumonia, the 66-year-old Russian leader seems eager to face a fresh one.
Naming Chubais first deputy prime minister is only the first move in the government reshuffle Yeltsin pledged on Thursday and more personnel changes are expected shortly.

A flurry of rumours and Kremlin leaks over the last week painted a picture in which the cabinet would be streamlined, more conservative figures would be either demoted or dismissed and Chubais would be left in overall charge of the economy.
Interfax news agency said on Friday Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and Chubais would be given a free hand to form an effectively new government.

Yeltsin's decision to appoint Chubais follows his key-note speech to parliament in which he made clear his concern that crime, corruption and economic stalemate threatened the state itself -- and consequently his own grip on power.
Many experts praised Yeltsin's position but said the key thing was to turn words into deeds. Yeltsin has apparently decided that Chubais was the man to do exactly that.
The track-record of the 41-year-old ginger-haired economist shows he may serve the purpose.
Between 1991 and 1996 Chubais pushed through privatisation like a rhinoceros, ignoring furious attacks by the opposition. Despite obvious drawbacks, it was carried through.
In 1996 Chubais effectively ran Yeltsin's re-election campaign, starting from a nearly zero rating. Yeltsin won in a run-off but with a comfortable lead.

Now the tasks facing Chubais appear enormous. In the short-term, he has to deal with a vicious circle of non-payment of taxes and consequent delays of salaries and pensions which is strangling the economy and plunging millions into despair.

He also has the task of uprooting economic crime and corruption -- something the opposition says he is part of -- and which Yeltsin said has reached top levels of power and threatens the state itself.

In the longer term, Chubais has to launch a restructuring of the economy and prepare the ground for at least a small amount of growth -- the second stage of reforms following the government's successful fight against inflation.
Some experts say the reshuffle could free Chernomyrdin from everyday running of the economy and allow him to become Yeltsin's heir-apparent for the presidential election in 2000.
Chubais will undoubtedly help unite most Russian reformers, probably with the exception of the Yabloko grouping headed by Grigory Yavlinsky.
His appointment is sure to be hailed by the West and, probably coincidentally, U.S. President Bill Clinton gave an optimistic prognosis for the Russian economy on Friday.
But political risks at home are great.
Chubais, deeply unpopular with the millions impoverished by radical market reforms, is public enemy number one for the communists and their allies in the State Duma lower house of parliament.
He will be running against time in trying to accelerate payments of overdue salaries and pensions ahead of a nationwide day of protest the opposition scheduled for March 27.

The communists say they will also try to muster enough votes for a no-confidence motion in the government. If it is voted through twice, Yeltsin will have the choice of dismissing either the cabinet or the Duma itself.
But a fresh election might return an even more hostile Duma in a country where people's patience is running short.
